title: Myths and Folk Tales
description: Ten calm retellings of folk tales from the United States and Britain, from Paul Bunyan, Johnny Appleseed and Rip Van Winkle to the selkie, the sword in the stone, Brer Rabbit, the Jersey Devil, Pecos Bill and the Green Man, each with a note on where the tale comes from.

lessons.title: Paul Bunyan and Babe the Blue Ox
lessons.summary: The tall tales of the logging camps, the giant and his blue ox, and the statues that carry the legend today.
lessons.text:
In the logging camps of the northern United States and Canada, winter evenings were long. After a day of cutting pine in the snow, the men sat around the stove and told stories about Paul Bunyan, the greatest giant who ever swung an ax. The tellers were overwhelmingly working men, not writers, and each one added a detail of his own. Whoever told the biggest lie with the straightest face won the evening.

Paul, they said, was so large as a baby that it took five birds to carry him to his parents. As a grown man he outweighed a hundred of his workers, and his footprints, filled with rain, became the ten thousand lakes of Minnesota. Once he let his heavy ax drag behind him, and it cut a gorge so deep and wide that people now call it the Grand Canyon. The tellers loved that gorge: such a grand lie about such a real place.

Paul's companion was Babe, a blue ox. Babe had been an ordinary white calf until the Winter of the Blue Snow, when the cold turned him blue forever. He grew so swiftly that each morning Paul found the barn a little smaller around him. Babe was invaluable to the camp. He could pull a whole forest of logs down to the river, and when a logging road twisted like a snake, he pulled it straight in an afternoon. In usefulness, the men agreed, that invaluable ox outweighed all their tools put together.

Feeding the crew was a task of its own. The cook made pancakes on a griddle so wide that nobody could see across it. To grease it, the kitchen boys tied bacon to their boots and glided round and round like skaters on a frozen pond. A good skater could grease the whole griddle before breakfast.

The legend did not stay in the woods. Early in the twentieth century, a lumber company began to use Paul and Babe in its advertising. The public response was overwhelmingly warm, and the stories traveled swiftly into newspapers and children's books. Towns in Minnesota then built enormous statues of the pair. In Bemidji, the first Babe is said to have been built on a truck chassis, so that the ox could be driven through the streets in a winter parade, with the high school pep band marching behind. That chassis is long gone. When such statues need repair today, workers may spend days welding new steel inside the old shapes, and the welding sparks fly like the snow in the old stories. Near Brainerd, a seated Paul even greets children by name. He is a robotic giant, and his robotic voice gives young visitors the kind of pep talk they expect from a hero.

Questions:
Who told the first stories about Paul Bunyan?
The tellers were overwhelmingly working men in the logging camps, not writers.
How was the gorge in the story made?
Paul let his heavy ax drag behind him, and it cut a gorge that people now call the Grand Canyon.
Why was Babe invaluable to the camp?
He could pull a whole forest of logs to the river, and he could pull a twisting road straight.
How was the giant griddle greased?
Kitchen boys tied bacon to their boots and glided round it like skaters on a frozen pond.
Why was the first Babe in Bemidji built on a truck chassis?
It was built that way so that the ox could be driven through the streets in a parade.

lessons.title: Johnny Appleseed
lessons.summary: The real John Chapman planted apple nurseries ahead of the settlers, and the legend of the gentle wanderer grew from his life.
lessons.text:
Every child in the United States knows the picture: a cheerful man with no shoes and a cooking pot on his head, wandering through the wilderness and throwing apple seeds from a sack. The picture is charming but unrealistic. The real Johnny Appleseed was a careful businessman as well as a gentle wanderer, and his story is radically different from the cartoon.

His name was John Chapman. He was born in Massachusetts in 1774, and as a young man he walked west into Pennsylvania and Ohio, where new settlers were clearing land. Chapman understood the frontier. Under some land rules, a settler had to plant an orchard to keep his land, and young apple trees were hard to find. So Chapman traveled in the vanguard of settlement, a few years ahead of the farmers. He collected seeds from cider mills, chose good ground along a river, planted a nursery, and built a fence around it to keep the deer away. By the time the settlers arrived, his young trees were ready. To be in the vanguard, for him, did not mean to lead an army; it meant to be waiting with a gift.

He could not stay to tend every nursery, so he left each one with a caretaker, usually a neighbor, who sold the trees for him. He returned now and then to see how the caretaker was managing, and he was patient with buyers who had no money. Many paid with old clothes or a meal, and many more made a deferred promise to pay after the harvest. Some deferred payments were never made, and Chapman seems not to have minded.

His trees did not produce the sweet, shiny apples of a modern supermarket. Apples grown from seed are unpredictable, and most are small and tart. Tart apples, however, made excellent cider, the everyday drink of the frontier.

Chapman was certainly quirky. He often went without shoes, even in cold weather, and he slept outdoors, waking in the dew under the trees. He followed the religious ideas of a Swedish thinker, Emanuel Swedenborg, and his personal ethic was one of simplicity and kindness. Stories of that ethic spread widely: he would not hurt an animal, and he gave away much of what he earned. Some of these quirky stories may be exaggerated, but people told them while he was still alive.

He died in Indiana in 1845, owning land and many nurseries, yet living as simply as ever. After his death the legend changed him radically, until the careful businessman became the singing figure of children's films. An unrealistic legend can still hold a true heart, however. On a spring morning, when the dew lies on an old orchard, it is pleasant to remember the man who walked ahead of everyone else, carrying seeds.

Questions:
How is the popular picture of Johnny Appleseed unrealistic?
The real man was a careful businessman who planted nurseries, not a man throwing seeds at random.
Why did Chapman travel in the vanguard of settlement?
He wanted his young trees to be ready when the settlers arrived and needed them.
What did a caretaker do?
A caretaker looked after a nursery and sold the trees for Chapman.
Why were tart apples still useful?
Tart apples made excellent cider, the everyday drink of the frontier.
What was Chapman's personal ethic?
His personal ethic was one of simplicity and kindness.

lessons.title: Rip Van Winkle's Long Sleep
lessons.summary: A good-natured villager in the Catskill Mountains falls asleep for twenty years and wakes in a new country.
lessons.text:
In 1819, the writer Washington Irving published a story set in a village at the foot of the Catskill Mountains, in New York, where the descendants of Dutch settlers lived quietly beside the Hudson River. Irving presented it as an old local tale, and readers believed him so completely that the tale soon seemed older than the village itself.

Its hero, Rip Van Winkle, was a kind, cheerful man whom everybody liked. He would help any neighbor build a fence or carry a load, but his own farm was another matter. His avoidance of work at home was famous: a steady, good-humored avoidance of anything useful to himself. His fields were full of weeds, his wife complained about it, and their quarrels could be heard from one end of the village to the other. Rip did not brood over these quarrels. He was not a man who broods. He simply picked up his gun and walked into the hills, lest he be given another job, and lest his wife find him sitting still.

One autumn afternoon, high in the mountains, he met a group of strange little men in old-fashioned Dutch clothes. They were bowling in silence, and each time a ball rolled, the sound echoed through the hills like thunder. They offered Rip a drink, and he accepted. Soon his eyes grew heavy. He tried to resist, but he succumbed to the deepest sleep of his life, as a tired traveler succumbs to the warmth of a fire.

When he woke, the morning sun was shining. His beard reached his belt, his gun was covered in rust, and his joints and ligaments were so stiff that every step hurt. In the village nobody knew him. The portrait of King George on the inn's sign had become a portrait of General Washington, and men were holding a noisy quarrel about elections. At last a young woman with a brood of small children recognized him as her father. People had long since stopped asking about his whereabouts, and most had decided that his whereabouts would never be known. Rip had slept for twenty years. In the ensuing days, he slowly understood that the country had fought a revolution while he lay under a tree.

He settled down happily. He found a rocker on the porch of the inn, and from that rocker he told his story to every traveler, until the ensuing generations knew it by heart.

Modern readers sometimes ask whether such a sleep is possible, and the physiological answer is no. A body that did not move for twenty years would lose its muscles, and its ligaments would tighten until walking was impossible. The physiological details hardly matter, however. What stays with us is the picture of a man waking in a world that has moved on without him, and making himself at home in it.

Questions:
Why was Rip's wife unhappy with him?
She was unhappy because of his avoidance of work on his own farm.
Why did Rip walk into the hills?
He walked into the hills lest he be given another job.
What happened after Rip accepted the drink?
His eyes grew heavy, and he succumbed to a deep sleep.
Who recognized Rip in the village?
A young woman with a brood of small children recognized him as her father.
Is such a long sleep possible?
The physiological answer is no: a body that did not move for twenty years would lose its muscles, and its ligaments would tighten.

lessons.title: The Selkie of the Northern Isles
lessons.summary: In Orkney and Shetland, islanders told of seals who become people on land, and of a selkie woman who married a fisherman.
lessons.text:
Far to the north of Scotland lie the islands of Orkney and Shetland, low and green, with more sky than land. For centuries they belonged to the kings of Norway, and their people spoke a Nordic language called Norn. Even after the islands passed to Scotland, many islanders remained bilingual for generations, speaking Scots at the market and Norn at home. Their stories were bilingual too, a mix of Nordic and Scottish traditions, and one of the best loved is the tale of the selkie.

Selkies, the islanders said, are seals in the sea and people on land. On certain clear nights they swim to a quiet beach, take off their sealskins, and dance on the sand in human form. Gray seals are common around the islands, and anyone who has met their large dark eyes will understand the idea. Seals are also curious about music. A person who sings on the shore can often entice them closer, and old people said that you could entice a selkie by shedding seven tears into the sea.

In the most famous version, a young fisherman was walking home along the shore one night when he saw a group of selkies dancing. The water sparkled behind them in the moonlight. He picked up one sealskin and hid it under his coat. When the dancers ran back to the sea, one young woman could not find her skin and was left behind, marooned on land. The fisherman was kind to her, and in time she agreed to marry him. They had children, and the family lived happily enough. Yet she remained marooned between two worlds, and every evening she walked down to the wharf and watched the waves.

One day, years later, her youngest child found the old skin in a chest and asked what it was. She knew at once. She held her children for a long time, and then she went back to the sea. The tale does not end in sorrow, however. On calm mornings, the family found fresh fish left on the rocks beside the wharf, and a gray seal often watched the children from the waves.

The story is uniquely suited to the islands, where every family lived between the fields and the ocean. It is uniquely gentle, too: nobody in it is wicked, and its sadness is the sadness of loving two homes at once.

Visitors to the islands can still feel that double life. In late summer, tiny algae in the water sometimes give off light when a boat passes, so that the dark sea seems to sparkle with blue stars. Fishermen have long known these algae, and it is easy to imagine the selkies dancing by their light. In the island towns, jewelers sell silver pendants in the shape of a seal, and many travelers buy a pendant to remember the selkie by.

Questions:
Why were many islanders bilingual?
They spoke Scots at the market and Norn, a Nordic language, at home.
How could a person entice seals closer?
A person who sings on the shore can often entice them closer.
Why was the selkie woman marooned on land?
The fisherman had hidden her sealskin, so she could not return to the sea.
How did the story end?
She returned to the sea, but the family found fresh fish on the rocks beside the wharf.
Why is the story uniquely gentle?
Nobody in it is wicked, and its sadness is the sadness of loving two homes at once.

lessons.title: The Sword in the Stone
lessons.summary: A young helper pulls a sword from a stone in a London churchyard and becomes King Arthur, in a test without battle.
lessons.text:
Most people know the scene even if they have never opened the old books: a sword standing upright in a block of stone, a crowd of knights who cannot move it, and a boy who draws it out as easily as a spoon from a jar of honey. The scene first appears in a French poem written around 1200, and it reached English readers through Thomas Malory's great book of Arthur's life, printed in 1485.

In Malory's telling, the old king has died, and nobody knows who should rule. The country is close to war, so the wise Merlin and the archbishop work in tandem to find a peaceful answer: Merlin provides the wonder, and the archbishop, working in tandem with him, makes it lawful. On Christmas morning, a stone appears in a London churchyard with a sword fixed in it, and on it are written words: whoever pulls it out is the true king. One by one, the proud lords try, and the sword does not move.

On New Year's Day there is a tournament, and among the riders is a young knight, Sir Kay, with his foster brother Arthur as his helper. Arthur is a novice, too young to fight. On the way, there is a small snag: Kay has left his sword at their lodgings. Arthur rides back to fetch it, but the house is locked. The snag seems serious until Arthur remembers the sword in the churchyard. He pulls it out without effort and carries it to his brother.

Kay recognizes the sword and, for a moment, claims the honor for himself. Admittedly, this is not his finest hour, but he soon tells the truth. Their father makes Arthur put the sword back and draw it again before witnesses. Even then the hurdles are not over. The lords cannot accept that a novice of unknown family should rule them, and Arthur has to draw the sword again at several feasts. Only after these hurdles are cleared is he crowned. Admittedly, the lords are slow, but the story is patient with them.

In many legends a hero proves himself in battle, and a dragon or a giant is slain. Nothing is slain here. The test is an initiation, but a gentle initiation: it asks only for the right person.

Later centuries kept returning to the scene. In nineteenth-century Britain, a countess might give a costume ball at which her guests came as Arthur and his knights, dancing across the ballroom in imitation armor, while the countess herself appeared as the Lady of the Lake. The ballroom glittered with candles. Today, gift shops sell imitation swords in plastic stones, yet in a small chapel in Italy a real sword stands in a rock, said to have been placed there by a knight about 850 years ago.

Questions:
Why do Merlin and the archbishop work in tandem?
They work in tandem to find a peaceful answer, because the country is close to war.
What is the small snag on the way to the tournament?
Kay has left his sword at their lodgings.
Why does Arthur face more hurdles after he draws the sword?
The lords cannot accept that a novice of unknown family should rule them.
Why is the test called a gentle initiation?
Nothing is slain, and the test asks only for the right person.
What might a countess do in nineteenth-century Britain?
She might give a costume ball at which guests danced across the ballroom in imitation armor.

lessons.title: Brer Rabbit and the Trickster Tradition
lessons.summary: The small, clever rabbit of the southern tales escapes the larger animals again and again, and his stories carry a long history.
lessons.text:
In the old stories of the southern United States, few characters are as clever as Brer Rabbit. "Brer" is an old way of saying "brother," and the animals of these tales all share it: Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox, Brer Bear and Brer Wolf. Brer Rabbit is small and weak, and the larger animals outnumber him in every tale. Again and again, Brer Fox plans to kidnap him, and every plan to kidnap him fails, because the rabbit thinks faster than the fox can run.

The tales were first told by enslaved Black people in the South, and their roots reach back to West and Central Africa, where a clever hare or a spider named Anansi plays similar tricks. Life under slavery was cruelly restrictive. People could not travel, learn or speak freely. In so restrictive a world, a story in which an outnumbered little animal defeats the strongest offered a quiet sense of empowerment. That empowerment was hidden in plain sight; to an outsider, it was only a story about animals.

The most famous tale shows how the trick works. Brer Fox makes a little figure out of sticky tar and sets it beside the road. Brer Rabbit comes along and says good morning. The tar figure says nothing. Brer Rabbit grows angrier and angrier, and at last he hits it, and his paw sticks fast. Here the rabbit is reactive, and his temper gets him caught. Then he stops reacting and starts thinking. He lets out a long groan. "Do anything you like with me," he begs, "but please don't throw me into the briar patch!" With every groan he sounds more frightened. The fox, who is reactive too and wants to do whatever the rabbit fears most, throws him straight into the thorny bushes. A moment later the rabbit calls out from safety: he was born and raised in a briar patch.

Other tales follow the same pattern. When a farmer's poultry go missing, the blame lands on Brer Rabbit, and he talks his way out of it. Even a noisy poultry yard becomes a stage for his quick mind.

The history of the written tales is more difficult. In 1880, Joel Chandler Harris, a white newspaper writer in Georgia, published the stories in a famous book. His books made Brer Rabbit known around the world, but they also complicate the history, because Harris surrounded the tales with a comfortable picture of plantation life that was far from the truth. Later writers, many of them Black, have told the tales in their own voices, and their versions usefully complicate the old picture.

Today, gentle versions appear in preschool picture books, and preschool children laugh at the briar patch without knowing how long the joke has lasted.

Questions:
Why is Brer Rabbit always in danger?
He is small and weak, and the larger animals outnumber him in every tale.
Why did the tales offer a sense of empowerment?
Life under slavery was cruelly restrictive, and in the tales an outnumbered little animal defeats the strongest.
How does Brer Rabbit get caught by the tar figure?
He is reactive, grows angry, hits the figure, and his paw sticks fast.
What does Brer Rabbit beg Brer Fox not to do?
With a long groan, he begs the fox not to throw him into the briar patch.
Why do Harris's books complicate the history?
Harris surrounded the tales with a comfortable picture of plantation life that was far from the truth.

lessons.title: The Jersey Devil
lessons.summary: A winged creature of the New Jersey pine forests began as an old insult and became a friendly local legend.
lessons.text:
In the south of New Jersey lies the Pine Barrens, more than a million acres of low pine forest, sandy roads and dark streams. It is a quiet place, and like many quiet places it has a legend: the Jersey Devil, a creature with wings, a long tail and the head of a horse, said to fly over the trees at night.

The oldest version of the story is set in 1735. A woman known as Mother Leeds, it says, already had twelve children, and when another was coming, she sighed that this one might as well be a devil. When the baby arrived, it grew wings and flew up the chimney. Historians suspect a more ordinary beginning. A real man named Daniel Leeds published popular almanacs in the area and argued loudly with his rivals, who called him a devil in print.

The legend may also owe something to smuggling. In the eighteenth century, the rivers and creeks of the Pine Barrens were ideal for smuggling goods past the tax collectors, and a story about a creature in the woods kept curious people at home after dark.

The great frenzy came in January 1909. For about a week, people around Philadelphia and across southern New Jersey reported strange footprints in the snow and a flying shape over the roofs. Some schools closed, and newspapers fed the frenzy with drawings. A reward was reportedly offered for the creature's capture, but nobody ever received a payout, because nobody captured anything. Two showmen did find their own kind of payout: they displayed a counterfeit devil, an ordinary kangaroo with green stripes painted on its fur and false wings attached to its back. Crowds paid to see the striped animal. The counterfeit was soon forgotten, but the striped kangaroo is now a favorite part of the story.

Scientists have never needed to refute the legend, because there is nothing to refute: no bones and no clear photographs. Some of the lights seen over the bogs may come from methane, a gas produced by rotting plants in wet ground, which can occasionally burn with a faint glow. Most sightings, however, come from tired drivers. On a quiet roadway through the pines, a large bird rising from a ditch can look like almost anything, and the black asphalt of the roadway makes the night seem even darker.

Today the Jersey Devil is less a fear than a friend. A professional hockey team is named after it. Children on evening walks shine a flashlight into the trees and laugh at every shadow the flashlight finds. Local newspapers still find blurry photos of wings in their inbox, and an editor may answer each message in the inbox with a smile. Methane and birds may explain the sightings, but the people of the Pine Barrens are glad to keep their devil, flying somewhere above the asphalt.

Questions:
How might the name of the Jersey Devil have begun?
Daniel Leeds argued loudly with his rivals, and they called him a devil in print.
How did smuggling help the legend?
A story about a creature in the woods kept curious people at home while smuggling went on.
Why did nobody receive a payout?
Nobody received a payout because nobody captured anything.
What was the counterfeit devil of 1909?
It was an ordinary kangaroo with green stripes painted on its fur and false wings on its back.
What may explain some of the lights over the bogs?
Some of the lights may come from methane, a gas produced by rotting plants in wet ground.

lessons.title: Pecos Bill Rides the Cyclone
lessons.summary: The tall tales of a Texas cowboy raised by coyotes, who tamed a snake and rode a storm.
lessons.text:
Texas has always been a land of big skies and bigger stories, and its tallest hero is Pecos Bill. Like Paul Bunyan, he lives in the kind of tale that nobody believes and everybody enjoys. The pleasure lies in the telling: the calm voice, the straight face, and the lie that grows with each sentence.

According to the stories, Bill was the youngest child of a large pioneer family moving west by wagon. As they crossed the Pecos River, the baby bounced out of the wagon, and nobody noticed. A family of coyotes found him and raised him as one of their own. For years Bill ran with the coyotes and believed he was one. Only when a passing cowboy pointed out that he had no tail did Bill agree, a little sadly, to become a human again.

He grew up to be the greatest cowboy in the West, tough to the marrow. Cowboys said that the desert sun had dried the very marrow of his bones into leather. He ate beans with a salsa so hot that it melted the spoon, and he asked for more salsa. When a scorpion once stung him, it was the scorpion that had to lie down and rest. Snakes were no trouble either. Bill met a huge snake with long fangs, tied it in friendly knots, and used it as a rope from that day on. The snake, they said, grew fond of him and kept its fangs to itself.

The most famous story is about a cyclone, a great spinning storm, that came across the plains. Bill jumped onto its back and rode it like a wild horse. The cyclone turned like the rotor of a giant machine, but Bill held on. At last the storm rained itself out over California, and Bill came down so hard that the ground sank below sea level and became Death Valley. Today we would call it a seismic event: had anyone owned seismic instruments in those days, the shock would surely have broken them all. Bill, of course, simply stood up and walked away, still turning a little, like a helicopter rotor slowing down.

Cowboys may have traded such tales in the adobe buildings of old trading posts. Adobe is a building material of sun-dried bricks made of earth and straw, and its thick walls stay cool in the heat, which made those rooms pleasant places for a story after a hot day.

Scholars, however, point out that Pecos Bill may owe more to writers than to cowboys. The first stories about him appeared in a magazine in the early twentieth century, and few old cowboys remembered hearing of Bill before then. That does not make him less loved. Today, at Texas fairs, a teller in a tall hat may describe the cyclone while families eat tacos and fresh salsa under the stars.

Questions:
Who raised Pecos Bill?
A family of coyotes found him and raised him as one of their own.
What happened when a scorpion stung Bill?
It was the scorpion that had to lie down and rest.
How did Bill use the snake?
He tied it in friendly knots and used it as a rope, and it kept its fangs to itself.
What happened when Bill came down from the cyclone?
He came down so hard that the ground sank and became Death Valley.
Why were adobe rooms pleasant places for a story?
Their thick walls of sun-dried bricks stay cool in the heat.

lessons.title: How Scholars Count Stories
lessons.summary: An archivist explains how folk tales are classified, cataloged and saved, from tale types to a digital archive.
lessons.text:
I work in a small archive of folk tales at a university, and visitors often ask me the same question: how can anyone keep order among thousands of stories that are told differently in every village? The answer, like most answers in academia, is a system, and the system has a long history.

For a long time, folk tales sat at the edge of academia. Professors studied poems and histories; old stories told by farmers seemed too humble. That changed in the early twentieth century, when scholars began to compare tales across countries and noticed that the same plots appeared everywhere. A Finnish scholar, Antti Aarne, published a list of tale types in 1910, and others expanded it over the following decades. Each type has a number. The story of a seal woman who marries a fisherman, for example, belongs with a family of tales about animal brides, and it has its own number in a separate list of northern legends.

The catalog is descriptive, not judging. A descriptive entry tells you what happens in a type of tale and where it has been found; it does not tell you which version is best. Another scholar, Vladimir Propp, went further and studied the syntax of stories. Just as a sentence has a grammar, he argued, a fairy tale has a syntax: a fixed order of steps, such as a hero leaving home, receiving a gift, and returning changed.

Our own archive holds recordings, the primary sources; studies about them, the secondary sources; and encyclopedias and guides, the tertiary sources, which summarize the work of others. Students usually begin with tertiary works and end, if they are lucky, with the voices themselves.

When we built a digital catalog, the aforementioned numbers caused a small problem: both lists use plain numbers, and a bare number does not say which list it belongs to. The solution was a namespace. Each code now carries a short label showing which list it comes from, so that a number in one namespace can never be confused with a number from another. The aforementioned seal woman, for instance, can carry codes from both lists without confusion.

Our building also taught us about planning. Some years ago, workers found asbestos in the ceiling of our storeroom. Asbestos is harmless while it stays still but dangerous when disturbed, so every box had to be moved before the repairs. Fortunately, we had a contingency plan: copies of every recording were already kept in a second building, and the contingency plan included a timetable for moving the originals. We followed the timetable exactly, and nothing was lost.

Then, in 2020, came the lockdown. The building closed, but the work did not stop. During the lockdown, volunteers at home listened to old recordings online and typed out what they heard. When the doors opened again, we had more written texts than ever before.

Questions:
Why did folk tales sit at the edge of academia for a long time?
Professors studied poems and histories, and old stories told by farmers seemed too humble.
What does a descriptive entry in the catalog do?
It tells you what happens in a type of tale and where it has been found.
What are tertiary sources?
They are encyclopedias and guides, which summarize the work of others.
Why did the archive need a namespace?
Both lists use plain numbers, and a bare number does not say which list it belongs to.
What happened during the lockdown?
Volunteers at home listened to old recordings online and typed out what they heard.

lessons.title: The Green Man of English Churches
lessons.summary: A visitor goes looking for the leafy carved faces hidden in the roof of an old village church.
lessons.text:
The church stood at the end of a narrow lane, gray and low, with a square tower and a graveyard of leaning stones. As I opened the gate, the clock in the tower struck eleven, one deep bong after another, and the last bong hung in the still air.

I had come to see the Green Man. Across England, in hundreds of old churches and cathedrals, stone carvers of the Middle Ages left the same strange image: a human face made of leaves, or a face with leaves and branches growing from its mouth. Nobody knows exactly what it meant to the people who carved it. The name itself is modern: a writer, Lady Raglan, gave it in 1939.

Inside, the church was cool and smelled of old wood. A friendly woman who looked after the building was arranging flowers by the door. When I explained why I had come, she smiled, took a flashlight from a drawer, and led me forward. On the way she dropped a coin into the collection box, and it landed with a small, bright ting. Then she pointed the flashlight up at the roof, and her ring tapped its metal case with another small ting.

There, at the point where the wooden beams crossed, was a carved face. Oak leaves grew from its lips and curled across its cheeks, and its eyes looked sideways, as if it had just noticed something amusing at the far end of the church. A second face peered sideways in the other direction, so that the two seemed to be sharing a joke.

The woman told me that the carvers often copied real plants, such as oak and ivy. Many of them were medicinal plants, used by monks and village healers for teas and cures, so the faces may also be a kind of garden of medicinal knowledge. Admittedly, this is only one theory. Others see the Green Man as a symbol of spring and new life. Some people once called him an ancient forest god, but most historians now doubt it. Admittedly, the face keeps its secret well.

It is remarkable that so many Green Men survived at all. During the Reformation, about 500 years ago, many images in English churches were removed or broken, because the new church leaders rejected them. The faces in the roof, however, were too high, too small and perhaps too harmless to bother with, so the Reformation largely passed them by.

As we stood there, the sun came out from behind a cloud. Light poured through the old glass, and the carved leaves seemed to brighten and almost move. I watched the face brighten until it looked nearly alive. Outside, the clock struck the half hour with a single bong. A small bird sang in the hedge, and I walked back down the lane feeling that the Green Man had been glad of the company.

Questions:
What is the Green Man?
It is a carved human face made of leaves, or a face with leaves growing from its mouth.
What did the woman do with her coin?
She dropped it into the collection box, and it landed with a small, bright ting.
Which way did the carved faces look?
They looked sideways, as if they were sharing a joke.
Why might the faces be a garden of medicinal knowledge?
The carvers often copied medicinal plants that monks and village healers used for teas and cures.
Why did many Green Men survive the Reformation?
They were too high, too small and perhaps too harmless to bother with.
